html:
The common messes of Sparta, where citizen men ate their evening meal together in groups of about fifteen. Crete had a similar system.

Every Spartan man belonged to one from early adulthood. Each month he paid in a set amount of barley, wine, cheese and figs, plus a little money. This food came from the land worked by his helots. A man who could not pay lost his place in the mess, and with it his full citizenship as one of the "equals". As wealth gathered into fewer hands over the centuries, more Spartans dropped out, and the number of full citizens shrank.

The messes were also military units in small. Men who ate together fought together, and boys from the agoge were brought to listen and learn. The famous Spartan black broth was served there.

Unlike the Athenian symposium, where rich men drank at private parties, the Spartan mess made every citizen eat plainly at a common table, a pillar of the order laid down in the Great Rhetra.
sum: The common messes of Sparta, where citizen men ate their evening meal together in groups of about fifteen. Crete had a similar system.
